lectures.title: How to choose a Linux Distribution?

cues.en: I want to finish this chapter with the Or by answering the question How should you use a Linux distribution?
And first of all, what I would recommend is that you write down the requirements.
What do you need?
So, for example, do you need commercial support?
If so, for how many years until you are ready to jump to the next version?
Are you willing to pay for a license here?
Do you need tools like Linux or do you use specific software that requires a specific distribution,
or are there any additional requirements?
As an example, maybe you want to deploy a NodeJS application and that relies on a recent version of
NodeJS, maybe one of the distributions still ships with an outdated version there, and it can't run
your software by default.
In that case, you would need to install a more recent version of NodeJS manually, but then maybe this
will later cause some dependency issues and maybe this might be a reason why you might prefer a different
Linux distribution so that you do not run into those problems.
Or maybe you are using a software from a specific vendor that's proprietary and the vendor is like,
Yeah, this software works perfectly only with, let's say for example, Red Hat, Enterprise Linux.
And in that case, if you wanted to rely on commercial support of that third party, you might be required
to actually use Red Hat Enterprise Linux in case you, let's say something breaks, you want to be able
to sue that other company or whatever is defined in that contract.
So those would be requirements that you would need to find out or that you would need to analyze when
you want to choose your Linux distribution.
After this, you can evaluate, you can try to run the same program on two different distributions.
Most of them will feel quite similar, but maybe you like one more or one just works better again,
for example, because of version differences.
Or maybe if you are running PHP, certain additional features, the PHP modules that extend this programming
language are only available for certain distributions, and for others you might need to compile them
yourself.
And then again, this would be something that you would need to analyze and that might really influence
your decision there.
So this would be my tip here.
There is no right or wrong here.
Usually lots of Linux distributions can do their job.
I mean, they all build on top of the Linux kernel.
They all use GPL software to run it.
It's not like they are completely different.
Nonetheless, there are differences that do matter.
And your goal would be then, if your task is to choose a Linux distribution to choose the appropriate
one based on the requirements.
Again, if requirements are missing, usually you would be able to add those manually into an existing
distribution, but it usually might lead to potential problems there.
So it's better to choose a Linux distribution that matches your requirements as closely as possible.
So unfortunately, I'm unable to give you a clear answer here, but I hope this is still a great guideline
that will help you choose the correct Linux distribution for your job.
Nonetheless, all of them are quite similar.
And after this course or now that we are here, you have pretty much watched all the course here.
You will feel extremely familiar no matter which Linux distribution you choose.
So I think you are well prepared to manage even a system or a distribution that we haven't looked into
here in this course.
